title: Targeting the LIFR-LCN2 pathway to improve liver cancer therapy
text:
The current systemic therapies for liver cancer, including sorafenib and the combination of atezolizumab (anti-
PD-L1) and bevacizumab (anti-VEGF), have limited therapeutic benefits with no predictive biomarkers available.
Our preliminary studies uncovered roles for a targetable LIFR−NF-κB−LCN2 pathway in regulating liver
tumorigenesis, sorafenib-induced ferroptotic cell death, and tumor infiltration by cytotoxic T cells. The goal of this
project is to provide new insights into the mechanisms of therapeutic targeting of an iron-sequestering pathway,
which has significant clinical implications in regard to the biomarkers and therapeutic targets for liver cancer.

title: Functional Viromics of Betacoronavirus Entry
text:
Coronaviruses such as SARS-CoV-2 originate in animals and transmit to humans. New coronaviruses are
discovered and sequenced from wildlife frequently, but, without effective laboratory tools to study these viruses,
little is known about the zoonotic risk they pose to humans. We have developed several laboratory-based
platforms to characterize the cell entry for hundreds of betacoronaviruses and propose to use these tools to
annotate the ever-growing virome.

title: Mechanism of acid signaling in bone organ metastases on tumor and myeloid cell evolution towards immune suppression and tumor progression
text:
While immune therapy provides long-lasting remissions and even cures many cancers, it is significantly less
effective in breast cancer with only 5-6% of metastatic breast cancer patients even being eligible for
immune therapy. To address this, we present a new approach to stop breast cancer bone metastases (and
its painful sequelae) and overcome immune therapy resistance by blocking acid signaling in tumor and
immune cells in bone. This proposal could significantly impact breast cancer patients across subtypes.

title: Project 1: Definition of the structural principles underlying broadly protective humoral immunity to coronaviruses
text: PROJECT SUMMARY – PROJECT 1: Definition of the structural principles underlying broadly protective humoral immunity Although the COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated the development of SARS-CoV-2 vaccines at an unprecedented pace, no licensed vaccines elicit broad protection against a large spectrum of human coronaviruses. There is therefore an urgent need for vaccines inducing broad protection against currently circulating and distantly related betacoronaviruses for pandemic preparedness. The proposed Project aims to identify epitopes targeted by cross-reactive and broadly neutralizing anti-betacoronavirus antibodies to obtain an antigenic map of targets present at the surface of betacoronavirus spike trimers to guide our vaccine design efforts. Broadly neutralizing sarbecovirus antibodies recognizing the spike receptor-binding domain have recently been discovered, however, they do not cross-react with members of other subgenera. Previous studies have shown that the spike fusion machinery (S2 subunit), which is more conserved than the S1 subunit, harbors conserved epitopes targeted by cross-reactive polyclonal antibodies. Although a few β-coronavirus cross- reactive monoclonal antibodies are known, a deep understanding of the diversity of epitopes targeted by broadly neutralizing antibodies and their quantitative contribution to neutralization is lacking, thereby hindering the rational design of vaccines eliciting broad immunity. We will use three approaches to determine the molecular determinants of broad antibody-mediated coronavirus immunity by unveiling the types, specificities, and diversity of broadly neutralizing antibodies targeting all three main betacoronavirus subgenera (sarbecovirus, merbecovirus, and embecovirus). First, we will characterize the binding and neutralizing breath of polyclonal sera from nonhuman primates immunized with nanoparticle vaccines co-displaying multiple different RBD- and spike-based antigens. Second, we will determine the epitope specificities of cross-reactive antibodies in these sera using serological assays and by directly visualizing polyclonal antibodies in complex with vaccine-matched and heterologous antigens using cryo-electron microscopy. Finally, we will isolate monoclonal antibodies from nonhuman primates immunized with multivalent nanoparticle vaccines and characterize their structures at high resolution as well as their binding, neutralizing, and protective breadth.

title: Insular-Amygdala Conflict Processing After Voluntary Abstinence
text:
While individuals with Opioid Use Disorder (OUD) may voluntarily abstain from drug use due to negative
consequences or positive alternatives, relapse rates remain strikingly high. We will use conflict relapse models
that incorporate decisions between opioid use and negative consequences or positive alternatives so that we
can resolve the specific conditions that engage brain circuits that are active neuromodulation targets for the
treatment of Substance Use Disorder.

title: Atrial Fibrillation Post-GWAS: Mechanisms to Treatment
text:
OVERALL COMPONENT
NARRATIVE
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is an increasing clinical problem, and despite identification of strong genetic connections,
genetic findings have yet to achieve clinical applications. This Program aims to advance AF genomic
discoveries toward the bedside, focusing on genes to mechanisms, genes to drugs, and interactions of genes
with metabolism and environment. The 4 highly integrated projects and cores aim to bridge basic research in
AF towards clinically actionable therapies.

title: Statistical methods for spatial proteogenomics data in Alzheimer's disease
text:
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a major public health challenge, yet its progression at the cellular level remains
poorly understood. This project will develop innovative spatial proteogenomics methods to analyze cellular organi-
zation and interactions in AD, enabling deeper insights into disease mechanisms. By improving image annotation,
statistical modeling, and spatial inference, this project will facilitate the discovery of novel therapeutic targets and
advance precision medicine for neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Improving the Accuracy of Lupus Nephritis Diagnosis using Biomarkers Derived from Ultraviolet and Mid-infrared Spectroscopic Imaging
text:
Diagnosis of lupus nephritis (LN) using conventional histopathology is challenging and fraught with pitfalls. We
propose combining histopathology with information from two independent optical imaging modalities that provide
additional biochemical and macromolecular context to LN diagnosis. We develop a multi-modal histology
platform to collect co-registered images and combine data using a deep learning architecture to improve the
accuracy of LN diagnosis.

title: Harnessing Glycoproteomics and Glycomics to Understand Cardiac Biology and Disease
text:
Our research program develops and applies innovative mass spectrometry technologies, bioinformatics tools,
and methodologies to transform our understanding of cell surface proteins and glycans and answer outstanding
questions in stem cell biology and cardiac pathology. Our platforms promote the development of new reagents
and strategies to enhance the utility and function of pluripotent stem cell derived cardiomyocytes for a wide range
of research and clinical applications and promote the discovery of new strategies for treating advanced heart
failure.

title: The Role of Clonal Hematopoiesis in Lung Cancer: Immune Dysregulation and Therapeutic Targeting
text:
Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide, yet the role of clonal hematopoiesis
(CH) in lung cancer progression remains poorly understood. This study will investigate how CH mutations
promote immune suppression and identify new therapeutic strategies to improve immunotherapy response in
CH+ patients with lung cancer. Findings from this research may lead to better risk stratification and novel
treatment approaches for lung cancer patients harboring CH mutations.

title: Advancing multimodal biologics to combat antibiotic resistance at mucosal surfaces
text:
Overall Project Narrative
Antibiotics have been revolutionary in curing bacterial infections for a century; however, many pathogens are
developing antimicrobial resistance (AMR) leaving no clinical options. The BCM CARBIRU will identify non-
antibiotic strategies to decolonize AMR pathogens from human mucosal surface to prevent and treat bacterial
infections, expanding the range of tools available to combat urgent AMR threats.

title: Core 3: Bioinformatics and Biostatistics Core
text:
The Bioinformatics and Biostatistics Core (Core 3) will serve as a focal point to provide comprehensive
biostatistical resource, to provide a new integrative computational platform to support the elucidation of roles of
GDH1, IAP/STING, and FAK in LKB1-deficient LUAD, and to develop and maintain a centralized data
acquisition and management system. Core 3 will allow investigators across all P01 projects and cores to have
a formalized, ongoing and collaborative interaction and arrangement with three key expertise areas in
biostatistics, medical informatics, and bioinformatics.

title: Borrelia burgdorferi genotypic diversity, pathogenesis, and host cellular responses
text:
Borrelia burgodorferi sensu stricto, a spirochetal bacterium and the causative agent of Lyme disease in the
United States, is transmitted from the bite of an Ixodes spp. tick. Genotypic fluctuations in outer surface proteins
help the bacterium evade the host immune system allowing it to invade and cause varying degrees of clinical
manifestations in humans. Our research will provide novel insights into the role of B. burgdorferi genetic diversity,
the effects different genotypes have on the host immune landscape and cellular responses, and will establish
key drivers and mechanisms that allow B. burgdorferi to elicit specific immune responses in hosts which will aid
in better diagnostic tests and therapeutic targets for Lyme disease treatment and public health initiatives.

title: Cellular, molecular and physical mechanisms of vitreous structural heterogeneity underlying posterior vitreous detachment
text:
Age-related changes in the vitreous can cause retinal detachment, which often leads to permanent vision
problems that affect quality of life. The goal of this project is to find out why the vitreous changes with age, so
that ways to prevent vitreous aging can be developed to prevent retinal detachment in high-risk individuals.

title: Elucidating the impact of receptor binding on seasonal influenza strains
text:
Influenza is an endemic, respiratory virus in humans that causes both worldwide pandemics and
hundreds of thousands of deaths each year. I will investigate differences in the structures of
seasonal influenza viruses as they adapt to infect cells. Characterizing influenza vaccine strain
structure may inform the development of targeted therapeutics against influenza infection in the
future.

title: Viral Production and CRISPR Engineering
text: Viral Production and CRISPR Engineering Core The NEI UCSD Center Core Grant for Vision Research Viral Production and CRISPR Engineering Core is focused on the production of adeno-associated virus (AAV) and lentivirus (LV) vectors to allow for genome engineering in vivo. Over the last several years, Shiley Eye Institute faculty have been heavily invested in using genetic tools like high-throughput functional genomic screening (e.g., Wahlin and Welsbie) and human genetics (e.g., Weinreb, Ayyagari, Borooah) to identify genes involved in various ophthalmic diseases, including glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and inherited retinal degenerations (IRDs). To be able to study the function of these genes in rodent models of disease, it is necessary to produce gain-of-function (GOF) and loss-of-function (LOF) conditions. By fusing Cas9 to transcriptional activators and repressors, technologies like CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) and inhibition (CRISPRi), as well as conventional Cas9-mediated mutagenesis, can be used to produce the necessary GOF and LOF conditions. Moreover, novel CRISPR technologies are being developed therapeutically to edit specific base pairs or rewrite larger sections of genome using homology-directed repair (HDR). The key to all of these is the viral delivery of genes encoding these large Cas9 proteins as well as optimized guide RNAs (gRNAs) that direct Cas9. Finally, AAV can be used to express cDNAs (independent of CRISPRs). In all cases, faculty are using a variety of outside cores for AAV production, resulting in high costs, variable quality and only a limited selection of reagents. The Viral Production and CRISPR Engineering Core has access to compact regulatory elements that can be used to create all-in-one AAV vectors that deliver Cas9 as well as guide RNAs. The Core has a suspension cell culture setup, AAV and LV HEK293F producer cells, Cytiva AKTA Pure fast protein liquid chromatography (FPLC) system and BioRad digital droplet PCR (ddPCR) system for AAV/LV production, purification and titering. There is a dedicated part-time technician and extensive know-how regarding AAV and CRISPR engineering that will be available to faculty.

title: Engineering host-determinants of novel gut Microviruses
text: Engineering host-determinants of novel gut Microviruses PROJECT SUMMARY Non-phiX-like Microviruses are small, single-stranded DNA viruses that are numerous, diverse, and poorly understood members of the human gut virome. Their simple genetic structure makes them amendable to manipulation of their host specificity, while their small size enables phage production via de novo synthesis of their genomes from in-silico data, followed by transformation of virus-generating DNA in the host. The Research Project Leader (RPL) has previously established a strong research program to study these elusive phages. Through investigation of their biology and ecological roles in microbiomes, he is poised to develop microviruses as a versatile tool for the targeted manipulation of the gut microbial community towards desired health outcomes such as staving off bacterial infections. Several obstacles must be overcome before practical applications of his research can be explored through R01 grant funding. The patterns and determinants of microviral host identity and specificity need to be understood, and the feasibility of re-introducing engineered phages into mixed microbial populations needs to be demonstrated. This proposal addresses these issues through three scientific aims: 1) Identifying natural hosts and establishing virus-host systems for major microvirus lineages of the human gut, 2) Establishing a system for targeted modulation of Microviridae host range, and 3) Re-introducing phages into controlled microbiomes for precise manipulation of microbial community composition. Success in these endeavors requires extensive experience in culturing and manipulating not only microviruses (the RPL’s expertise), but also with anaerobic hosts such as Bacteroides and Prevotella. Through the Oklahoma Center for Microbiome Research (OCMR) Anaerobic Microbiology Core and COBRE-facilitated mentorship by experts in virology, metagenomics, and biology of human gut microbes, as well as interactions with a wide range of researchers in the microbiome field, the RPL will have access to the technical infrastructure, intellectual expertise, and professional network needed to pursue these aims. The project is hence crucial to the RPL’s short and long-term career goals of attaining research independence in the form of an R01/R35 grant; establishing his laboratory as a leading institution in the research of microviruses; and developing microviruses as modular tools for a fully synthetic phage therapy platform.

title: 'Mosaicism in Human Tissues, from Telomere to Telomere to RFA-22-013: "Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues Program: Genome Characterization Centers."
text:
Precision genomic medicine depends on a complete understanding of genetic variation in normal individuals,
but current approaches fail to capture all the types of genetic variation, because they 1) do not measure
genetic variation in so-called “unmappable” regions of the genome, and 2) assume the genomes of every cell
in a single multicellular human are identical. The goal of our proposal “Mosaicism in Human Tissues, from
Telomere to Telomere” is to characterize multiple types of human somatic variation across the entire human
genome in a set of 10 tissues from 50 donors, and to work with other members of the network towards
producing a framework for understanding somatic variation in post-mortem, non-pathological human tissues.

title: Cell Surface Receptor Recognition and Membrane Fusion in Mammalian Fertilization
text:
Membrane fusion of sperm and eggs is pivotal in sexual reproduction, but its molecular mechanisms are
largely unknown. The proposed research will characterize the assembly and architecture of the sperm
fertilization membrane proteins, as well as identify and characterize new cell-surface interactions in
sperm-egg recognition, adhesion and fusion. Understanding the functional organizations of sperm-egg
interactions has direct impact on human fertility and reproductive health.

title: When genomes collide: using hybrid zones to transform our understanding of behavioral and speciation genetics.
text:
We will use our model system to characterize the genetic mechanisms that underlie seasonal rhythms,
including genes and molecular pathways that are conserved across animals. Since many human diseases
exhibit seasonal rhythms but cannot be examined at the same molecular level as our model, our project will
generate results that can be used to enhance human health. We will also use our model to shed light on the
molecular and evolutionary processes that generate individual- and population-level patterns in human disease
risk and are being used in personalized medicine to diagnose and treat human illness.
